SUBJECT. The eat-in kitchen of a small house in Decatur, Illinois, in 1990, in the evening, under a pendant lamp that is above and out of the picture. A seven-year-old girl sits at the kitchen table facing us squarely, seen level with her eyes from close across the table: her head and shoulders in the middle of the frame, her chest, her two forearms, and her two hands on the table edge at the very bottom of the picture. Her parents are standing behind her, one at each side, talking to each other over her head; we see only their bodies from the shoulders down to the hips at the left and right edges of the frame, and their hands. At the left, her father: a pale short-sleeved shirt with a pen in the chest pocket, a dark belt, pleated trousers, his bare right forearm reaching into the picture with the hand open, palm up, stopped in the air. At the right, her mother: a soft knitted cardigan open over a collarless blouse, one hand lifted, palm turned in, fingers loose, stopped in the air too. Behind the child's head: a double-hung sash window with the night outside, its sill, a chrome tap and the edge of the sink, a laminate counter, the corner of a wall cupboard at the upper left.

COMPOSITION. Follow image 1 exactly: the same camera, the same size and position of her head, shoulders and arms, the two adult torsos at the frame edges cut off at the shoulders by the top of the frame, their two raised hands, the window behind her head, the sill, tap and counter, the table edge along the bottom. Image 1 is only a layout drawing from a 3D model: replace its mannequins with the real people and its boxes with the real things, and do not keep its mechanical even line. The slab across the top of the child mannequin's head is only her fringe. The mannequins' hands are mitts and boxes: draw real hands with five fingers. No adult's head or face appears anywhere in the picture.

WHAT SHE IS DOING. One second ago she was drumming her fingers on the table and her eyes were wandering. Her mother has just asked a question about her, in a dialect she is not supposed to understand, and she has understood it. Everything has stopped for one beat. Her hands are frozen in the middle of a tap: the right hand arched, one finger still lifted a centimetre above the wood and not coming down. Her head is perfectly still, level, facing us squarely. NOTHING in her face has changed: her lips are together and level, her jaw loose, her brows resting, exactly as before; she is not smiling, not frowning, not startled, not posing for anyone; her eyebrows are not raised and her mouth is not open. The whole event is in her eyes. They have stopped moving. Both irises are exactly parallel, not converged on anything, aimed a little below our eye line and very slightly toward the left of the picture, at empty air above the middle of the table: she is looking at nothing, because she is listening. The eyes are wide open, dark and very bright, the upper lids a hair higher than at rest so that the whole round iris shows. It is the stillness of a child who has just heard something meant for someone else, and is working it out.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. The lamp is overhead, in front of her and above the frame; its pool of light falls on her and on the table. Image 2 is the lighting guide. In the light: her face, her fringe and the top of her hair, her sweatshirt, forearms and hands, the table edge, and the fronts and raised hands of the two adults at the sides. Those lit parts are NOT PAINTED with any wash: bare cream paper left blank, with only thin ink outlines. No yellow, no white paint, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom: light is simply where the brush did not go. Her face, in the light, is fully and normally painted on that bare paper: thin fine line, her own warm rosy flesh wash, the pink blush on her cheeks, dark irises, thick upper lashes, glossy black ink hair; the softest transparent warm umber shadow under her fringe, under her chin and beside her nose, no more. In each eye one small crisp round catch-light of bare paper, high in the iris (the lamp), in the same place in both eyes. The adults' clothes in the light are line on bare paper with no colour of their own. Everything behind them is out of the light, under one even transparent warm umber ink wash: the wall, the window frame and sill, the tap, the counter, the cupboard; the night panes of the window a deeper layer of the same umber, never black; the ink lines show through. The edge between wash and blank paper is a clean, slightly soft wet edge.

PEOPLE. THE GIRL. Little Jade at about age 7, Decatur, Illinois, 1990: a Chinese girl in first or second grade, with LARGE round dark eyes set wide apart, each with thick dark upper lashes; distinct, fairly strong, straight dark eyebrows; a tiny button nose; a small soft mouth; a round face with soft cheeks and a wide warm pink blush, the chin a touch longer than a small child's. Glossy jet-black hair (pure black ink, never brown): a light fringe of a few soft parted strands with the forehead showing between them, long side locks in front of the ears, a small half-ponytail tied high at the back of the crown with a dark band, the rest straight down to her shoulder blades. Clothes (1990 American Midwest, hand-me-down, plain): an oversized plain heather-grey crew-neck sweatshirt with the sleeves pushed up to the elbows, no print and no lettering; dark navy stirrup leggings; bare feet. Proportions of a seven-year-old: about five and a half heads tall, thin arms and legs, a big round head. She is 7: clearly older than 5 and clearly younger than 10. Use the front view at the top left of image 3 for her head, but with the mouth perfectly level, not smiling. Image 4 is her expression sheet: the head at the far left of its top row is her face at rest; use that mouth, those brows and those wide eyes, and none of the other heads.

THE PARENTS, bodies and hands only. Image 5 is her father's model sheet: his build, short-sleeved shirt with the pen in the pocket, belt, trousers. Image 6 is a sheet of his hands: the open palm at the top left is his raised hand here; his right wrist is bare (the watch is on his left). Her mother's hands are a swimmer's: strong, capable, short plain nails, no rings. Use the images for likeness only; repaint in this painting.

We are level with her eyes and very close: her face fills the frame, from the fringe at the top edge to the chin at the bottom edge, facing us squarely. Nothing else is in the picture: no room, no furniture, no other person, only the dark and her, and one thin strip of light.

COMPOSITION. Follow image 1 exactly: the same camera, the same very large head filling the height of the frame and sitting a little left of the middle, the eye on the LEFT of the picture a little left of centre and a little above the middle of the frame, the mouth low in the frame. The same thin diagonal strip of light: straight, narrow (about as wide as her eye is tall), running from the upper left down to the lower right at about forty degrees. It touches a few strands of hair at her temple at the upper left, crosses the eye on the LEFT of the picture and the bridge of her nose, ends on her cheek beside the nose, and shows once more as a short bar at the lower right corner, beyond her jaw, on the rough brick behind her. Image 1 is only a layout drawing from a 3D model: replace its mannequin head with the real child (the slab across the top of the head is her fringe), and do not keep its mechanical even line. At the far left edge one upright timber stud of the wall, barely visible. Image 6 is the earlier painting of this same shot, a few seconds before: repaint it exactly, the same child, the same head size, the same eye, the same drawing hand (thin ink outlines and flat transparent washes, no realistic modelling), the same deep indigo dark. Change only the strip of light and the mouth. IN THIS PAINTING the strip is wider than in image 6, about half as wide again, and all the extra width is on its LOWER side: its upper edge stays where it is, still crossing the eye on the LEFT of the picture; its lower edge now runs down across the cheek and the side of the nose and just takes in the corner of her mouth on the RIGHT side of the picture. So that one corner of the mouth, about a third of the lips, is in the light, and the rest of the mouth is in the dark.

WHAT SHE IS DOING. She is watching one tiny thing floating in the strip of light, a hand's width in front of her face. Her head is perfectly still. The eye in the light is wide open, bright and fixed, its dark iris almost in the middle of the eye, turned only a very little toward her nose and slightly down, resting on that near point, the way a child looks when she is counting something: wide with attention, not with fright, and not cross-eyed. Her brows are resting. Her mouth has opened a little to say something: the lips parted by the width of a fingertip, a breath held behind them, the jaw still, no teeth showing. No sound will come. Her eye has not left the light. She is not smiling and not frowning and not posing for anyone: all the life in the face is in that one eye. Do not draw the thing she is watching.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. Image 2 shows where the light is: only the thin diagonal strip (its white shapes). The strip is NOT PAINTED: bare cream paper left blank, with only thin ink outlines of what it crosses. No yellow, no white paint, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom: light is simply where the brush did not go. Its two edges are straight and parallel, each a clean, slightly soft wet edge. Everything else in the picture, nine tenths of it, is dark: a near-black indigo ink wash, laid in several transparent layers, soft and deep, with the paper grain and fibres still breathing through it and slow, cloudy variations in its depth; never flat black, never a solid fill. Her face outside the strip is almost as dark as the wall behind it, only one step lighter: a viewer finds it a moment after finding the eye. In that dark the rest of her is barely there, given only by a slightly paler edge or a slightly darker line: the curve of one cheek, the two brows, the nostrils, a few strands of hair. The OTHER eye, on the right of the picture, is nearly lost: a soft dark almond with the faint line of its upper lid and lashes, no white showing, no highlight, no catch-light, so that it cannot be seen where it is looking. The dark is a deep indigo-blue ink, cool, not brown; the little that shows of her skin in it is still warm under the glaze, not grey and not ashen.

THE ONE THING IN FULL DEPTH: the eye in the strip of light. It is the only thing in the picture painted in full colour and with the finest, most loving line: every upper lash drawn, the lid's fold, the wet lower rim, a deep brown-black iris with its darker ring and pupil, one small crisp catch-light of bare paper in it shaped like a short thin slit (the crack the light comes through), and on the bare-paper skin around it a breath of warm rosy flesh colour. Where the strip crosses the corner of her mouth, the lips there are drawn with the same care, in a soft natural rose, with the small dark gap between them. Nothing else in the frame has any colour of its own.

THE GIRL. Little Jade, 1988, age 5: a small Chinese girl with a big round head and a short round face, very full soft cheeks with a wide warm pink blush, a tiny button nose, a tiny soft mouth, and LARGE round dark eyes set wide apart, each with thick dark upper lashes; distinct, fairly strong, straight dark eyebrows. Small child proportions, a big round head. Use the images for likeness only; repaint her in this painting.

SUBJECT. A kitchen in Decatur, Illinois, 1990, a bright morning. A seven-year-old Chinese girl stands facing us, very close, head and shoulders, seen level with her eyes from where her seated mother's face is. Her mother's two hands come up into the picture from below and hold the child's face, pushing her cheeks up into the shape of a smile. Of the mother only the two hands, the wrists and the forearms in cardigan sleeves are in the picture. Behind the child: a plain kitchen wall, and at the far left edge the upright line of a door frame. Nothing else.

COMPOSITION. Follow image 1 exactly: the same camera, the child's head in the upper middle of the frame at the same size, her eyes two fifths of the way down, her shoulders leaving the frame at the bottom, the two adult forearms rising from the bottom edge left and right of centre and converging on her face. Image 1 is only a layout drawing from a 3D model: replace its mannequin with the real child (the slab across the top of the head is her fringe) and its mitts with real hands, and do not keep its mechanical even line. CORRECT ONE THING in image 1: there the hands meet under her chin; in the painting they are higher, ON HER CHEEKS, as in the top-middle study of image 4.

THE HANDS. Each of the mother's hands cups one side of the child's jaw, the four fingers lying along the jaw and under the ear, and the pad of each thumb is pressed on the soft cheek just beside a corner of the mouth, pushing up and a little outward. The two thumbs do not touch each other and are not under the chin: there is the whole width of the mouth between them. Under the thumbs the cheeks bunch up into two round cushions below the eyes and the closed mouth is dragged into a wide upturned curve: a smile made by someone else's thumbs. The hands are careful and fond, the way a mother straightens a collar; they are not gripping. Her hands: strong capable swimmer's hands with short plain nails, no rings, no jewellery; five fingers on each, carefully drawn. The cuffs of a soft knitted cardigan at her wrists.

WHAT THE GIRL IS DOING. She is trying to get out of it. Above the pushed-up smile her brows come down hard and together, with a small knot between them, deeper than a moment ago; her eyes have slid as far as they go toward the right side of the picture, both irises in the right corners of the eyes, looking for the way out; her head is pulling back and turning a little away from the hands toward that side, chin tucked, shoulders coming up, like a child squirming away from a face cloth. Only the woman's forearm and hand are in the picture, with the rolled edge of a cream blouse sleeve at the right edge: no more of her. Behind the hands: the lower right pane of an old four-pane window, its vertical glazing bar just right of the child's head, the wooden side of the frame at the far right, the wooden sill running across below, and a strip of plain wall at the right edge. Image 1 is an earlier take of this same painting, and it is right in camera, in the child (her head, hair, jacket, raised arm and pointing hand), the window, the sill, the frost fern, the light and the wash: paint the same picture again, everything the same size and in the same place, and change ONLY the woman's forearm and hand as described under ONE CORRECTION.

ONE CORRECTION to image 1. In image 1 the woman's forearm and hand are too heavy and too old: a thick arm, a broad thumb with wrinkled knuckles, creased skin. It must be the arm of the child's MOTHER, a slim, fit Chinese woman of thirty-five, exactly the hand and forearm of image 2 (its top right study is this very grip; its bottom right study is the colour): a slender wrist, a narrower forearm with smooth unlined skin, a long neat thumb with a short plain nail and no wrinkles, fine knuckles. Make the dishwater flush stronger: forearm and hand a clear pink-red, deepest at the knuckles, the thumb tip and the heel of the hand, still damp, with a few beads of water. The grip itself stays as in image 1: the thumb across the near side of the child's sleeve, the four fingers wrapped round the far side with their tips just showing past the sleeve's edge, the sleeve bunching a little under them. WHAT IS HAPPENING. The mother has run up the stairs from the restaurant kitchen and reached her child in one movement. Her right hand has closed on the child's right forearm, over the white sleeve, just below the wrist: four fingers wrapped round the far side of the small arm, the thumb across the near side, the soft sleeve bunching under the grip. It is the grip of someone moving a child out of danger at once: firm, fast and sure, the knuckles a little raised, and not cruel: the fingers hold, they do not dig or twist. The pull has only just begun. The child's hand has not understood yet: her index finger is still extended and has only just left the glass, a finger's breadth of air between fingertip and pane, the other fingers loosely curled. THE TWO HANDS. The mother's: a Chinese woman of thirty-five, strong capable hands with short plain nails, no rings, no jewellery. Her bare forearm and hand are washed a clear pink-red from hot dishwater, distinctly pinker than ordinary skin, deepest at the knuckles and fingertips, and still damp. The plain cream cotton blouse sleeve is pushed up above her elbow; its rolled edge shows at the right edge of the picture. The child's: a FIVE-YEAR-OLD's hand, small, soft and plump, short fingers, tiny nails, a dimple over each knuckle; her whole forearm is thinner than the woman's wrist. A 27-year-old Chinese woman, the host, stands with her back to a wall of bookshelves, facing us, seen level with her eyes from two metres away, from the waist up. Beside her at the right edge of the frame stands a tall young man with his back to us, reading the book spines. Behind them the wall is all books: at the left and centre a tall dark-wood bookcase filled edge to edge with uniform sets of thick reference volumes, and on one shelf beside her head a short run of small slim paperbacks; at the far right, behind the man, the start of a second, pale bookcase with books of every height, some leaning, some stacked flat. No book has a title: every spine is blank or carries at most one small abstract band or dot. A third person stands at the far LEFT edge of the frame, nearer to us than she is: her childhood friend, seen from behind in three-quarter back view, cut off by the left edge and the bottom edge, so that we see only the back of his head, one ear, his right shoulder and upper back. His head is turned toward her and dipped in a small nod: he knows what the patting means too.

COMPOSITION. Image 3 is an earlier take of this same picture, and it is right in everything: repaint it the same, her face, grin, mouth, glasses, hair, hand on his arm, the man at the right, the shelves, the shadows, and ADD the childhood friend at the left edge, taking up about the left sixth of the frame, in front of the shelves; he is not in image 1. Five fingers. Her other arm hangs at her side.

WHAT SHE IS DOING. She is patting his arm fast with her whole hand, the way she does when an idea has just delighted her and she cannot wait to say it, and she is singing the word "see" straight to us. Her head is squared to us and tipped a few degrees toward him. Both irises point exactly into the lens, wide and shining. Her eyebrows are up. Her mouth is open on a long "ee" with a real, wide grin in it: the lips stretched wide and parted, the corners pulled up and back, the upper teeth showing as one clean simple pale band, a thin dark gap under them, the lower lip full. The dark-wood shelves and uprights, the gaps above the books and the far corners are under the same dusk-violet wash, a little deeper. No black anywhere. She and he stand in the lamp light, so they are painted normally with no wash over them: her warm rosy flesh colour and the pink blush on her cheeks clear and fresh, never grey, never ashen. The same thin diagonal strip of light: straight, narrow (about as wide as her eye is tall), running from the upper left down to the lower right at about forty degrees. It touches a few strands of hair at her temple at the upper left, crosses the eye on the LEFT of the picture and the bridge of her nose, ends on her cheek beside the nose, and shows once more as a short bar at the lower right corner, beyond her jaw, on the rough brick behind her. IN THIS PAINTING the strip is wider than in image 6, about half as wide again, and all the extra width is on its LOWER side: its upper edge stays where it is, still crossing the eye on the LEFT of the picture; its lower edge now runs down across the cheek and the side of the nose and just takes in the corner of her mouth on the RIGHT side of the picture. The eye in the light is wide open, bright and fixed, its dark iris almost in the middle of the eye, turned only a very little toward her nose and slightly down, resting on that near point, the way a child looks when she is counting something: wide with attention, not with fright, and not cross-eyed. Her brows are resting. Her mouth has only just opened to say something: the lips have come apart by no more than the thickness of a pencil, a thin dark gap at the middle of the mouth, the lower lip soft and relaxed, the jaw not dropped; NO teeth, no tongue, not a gasp and not an 'oh' of surprise or fright. She was about to say a word and is holding it, with a breath, behind her lips. No sound will come. Her eye has not left the light and is exactly as in image 6: no wider, with no more white showing; she is attending, not afraid. The dark keeps the same cool deep indigo-blue as image 6, not brown. She is not smiling and not frowning and not posing for anyone: all the life in the face is in that one eye. Do not draw the thing she is watching.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. Image 2 shows where the light is: only the thin diagonal strip (its white shapes). No yellow, no white paint, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom: light is simply where the brush did not go. Its two edges are straight and parallel, each a clean, slightly soft wet edge. Everything else in the picture, nine tenths of it, is dark: a near-black indigo ink wash, laid in several transparent layers, soft and deep, with the paper grain and fibres still breathing through it and slow, cloudy variations in its depth; never flat black, never a solid fill. Her face outside the strip is almost as dark as the wall behind it, only one step lighter: a viewer finds it a moment after finding the eye. In that dark the rest of her is barely there, given only by a slightly paler edge or a slightly darker line: the curve of one cheek, the two brows, the nostrils, a few strands of hair. The OTHER eye, on the right of the picture, is nearly lost: a soft dark almond with the faint line of its upper lid and lashes, no white showing, no highlight, no catch-light, so that it cannot be seen where it is looking. The dark is a deep indigo-blue ink, cool, not brown; the little that shows of her skin in it is still warm under the glaze, not grey and not ashen.

THE ONE THING IN FULL DEPTH: the eye in the strip of light. It is the only thing in the picture painted in full colour and with the finest, most loving line: every upper lash drawn, the lid's fold, the wet lower rim, a deep brown-black iris with its darker ring and pupil, one small crisp catch-light of bare paper in it shaped like a short thin slit (the crack the light comes through), and on the bare-paper skin around it a breath of warm rosy flesh colour. His head is tipped forward and down: he is looking down at something low between them, out of frame, where her hand lies on his forearm. Facing him, right of centre, a little shorter than he is, stands a 27-year-old Chinese woman, the host, seen from the chest up in three-quarter view, her face turned toward him and up to him. Behind them the wall is all books: a dark-wood bookcase filled edge to edge with uniform sets of thick reference volumes on four shelves; right behind her head the upright where it meets a second bookcase; and beside her head a short run of small slim paperbacks. No book has a title: every spine is blank. A third person stands at the far RIGHT edge of the frame, nearer to us than she is: her childhood friend, seen from behind in three-quarter back view, cut off by the right edge and the bottom edge, so that we see only the back of his head, one ear, his left shoulder and upper back. Her eyes are on his face, both irises turned up and toward the left of the picture, to where his eyes are; they are very bright and visibly WET: a thin clear line of water stands along each lower lid, drawn as a fine line of bare paper just above the lower lashes, and has not fallen; the rims of the lids are a little pink, the lower lashes damp and clumped, the whites faintly pink at the corners. No tear on the cheek. She has just blinked it back and will have to again. Her brows are resting, soft, only the faintest lift at their inner ends; her upper lids are a little lowered, as lids are just after a blink. This is tenderness, not alarm: she is NOT startled, NOT frightened, NOT surprised, NOT worried; the eyes are not widened. She is moved, and very fond of him, and it has caught in her throat. Each eye glistens: besides the catch-light there is a second, smaller glint low in the eye where the water stands. Her head is perfectly still. She is not smiling and not crying: she is holding still so that it stays in.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. Three paper floor lamps stand behind us and light the two of them and the fronts of the books; everything the lamps do not reach is the night. Image 2 shows it: pale = lamp light, darker = shade. The lamp-lit book spines are NOT PAINTED: bare cream paper left blank, with only thin ink outlines for each book. No yellow, no white paint, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom: light is simply where the brush did not go. The lamps throw soft overlapping shadows of the two heads and shoulders onto the books behind and to the left of them, as in image 2: each shadow is one even transparent dusk-violet ink wash laid across the bare-paper books, the outlines showing through, with a clean, slightly soft wet edge and no outline; where shadows overlap the wash is one step deeper. Her face is in the lamp light and is painted normally with no wash over it: warm rosy flesh colour, the pink blush on her cheeks clear and fresh, never grey, never ashen. THE ONE THING IN FULL COLOUR is her face: it carries the finest, most careful line in the picture. She is drawn quietly, thin line and pale wash, nothing emphasised. The books stay line on bare paper or line under violet wash, with no local colour of their own.

The eye in the light is wide open, bright and fixed, its dark iris almost in the middle of the eye, turned only a very little toward her nose and slightly down, resting on that near point, the way a child looks when she is counting something: wide with attention, not with fright, and not cross-eyed. THE HANDS, kept very quiet. At the very bottom edge of the frame, at the lower right where the strip of light leaves the picture, and cut off by the bottom edge: the knuckles of an adult woman's hand closed round the child's small hand, holding it. A painting on cream xuan paper, wide 16:9, in one hand: fine-line baimiao ink outlines and transparent ink wash, the paper grain and a few long paper fibres showing through everywhere.

SUBJECT. One upstairs room of a lilong house in Shanghai, a summer afternoon in 1986, seen from the eye height of a three-year-old sitting on the floor and looking steeply up, with a wide view: four adults by the door are laughing, and from down here they tower. Their legs, hands, hems and the things they hold are large and near; their heads are small, far up under the ceiling. From left to right: (1) at the far left, a grandmother sitting on the edge of a wooden bed, bent forward with laughing, in a short-sleeved cotton blouse printed with small indigo flowers on white and loose black trousers ending above the ankle, a folding paper fan half open in the hand that hangs toward us at the lower left; (2) beside her, a young aunt standing, in a pale dacron dress with a small collar and a hem just below the knee, her head thrown back, the back of one hand pressed to her mouth, the other hand hanging open; (3) in the middle, framed by the open doorway and farther away, the child's mother, smaller, standing on the threshold with one hand on the door frame; (4) at the right, a tall uncle in a white sleeveless cotton vest tucked into grey-blue twill trousers with a brown belt, leaning back with his chest and belly shaking, a white enamel mug with a lid and a dark-blue rim in one hanging hand, the other hand open and mid-slap toward his thigh. Above the two women at the left, the wooden frame of the bed's mosquito net and one diagonal bamboo pole; in the middle the plain wooden door frame with a dim landing beyond; at the right a tall dark wardrobe with a mirror door; above everything the plaster ceiling and its corner.

COMPOSITION. Follow image 1 exactly: the same camera, the same steep upward perspective, the same positions and sizes of the four figures, their hands, the door frame, the net frame, the wardrobe and the ceiling line. Image 1 is only a layout drawing from a 3D model: replace its mannequins with the real people and its boxes with the real things, and do not keep its mechanical even line. The mannequins' mitts are not hands: paint real hands with five fingers doing what is described. The slab in the lower left hand is the folding fan; put the enamel mug in the right-hand man's hand that hangs at the far right.

WHAT THEY ARE DOING. They are howling with laughter at something the child has just said, and none of it is explained to her. The laughter is all in the bodies, and it is big: the grandmother rocks back on the edge of the bed with one hand slapped on her knee and the fan dangling from the other; the aunt is doubled up sideways, one knee giving, the back of her hand jammed against her mouth; the uncle leans far back from the waist with his belly pushed out and shaking, his free hand caught in mid-slap on his thigh, the mug tilting in the other. Shoulders are up round their ears. A few quick repeated contour lines may show a shaking shoulder or belly, but no motion lines and no symbols.

WHO HAS A FACE. All three laughing heads are THROWN BACK, so that from down here we see each of them only from underneath: the stretched throat, the underside of the chin and jaw, an ear, the edge of the hair. Their faces are turned up toward the ceiling, away from us, and cannot be seen at all: there is no front of a face in view on the grandmother, the aunt or the uncle, so there are no eyes, no nose, no mouth, no teeth to draw, and no smooth empty face either. What little shows of each head, throat, jaw line, ear, hair line, is drawn in a few thin pale lines under the same wash as the wall and ceiling behind it, fainter than everything below it, like part of the picture the painter has not reached yet. Not a mask, not a white oval, not a blur. Only the mother's face is drawn, small and far away in the doorway, in shade: she is laughing too, more quietly, eyes narrowed with it behind her round glasses, mouth open in a short laugh, looking down at the child.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. The window and its sunlight are behind us; the child sits in the light but these adults stand outside it. As image 2 shows, no direct light falls on anything in this frame: there is NO bare-paper light on any figure. The whole picture is in shade under one even transparent warm grey-green ink wash, lightest low down where light bounces up off the sunlit floor onto the hems, shins, hanging hands, the fan and the mug, and deepening upward to the heads and the ceiling, darkest in the doorway behind the mother; ink lines show through it everywhere and there is no black. The nearest things, the hanging hands, the fan and the enamel mug, are drawn with the finest and most careful line in the picture, the hands in a warm flesh wash under the glaze; the higher up a figure goes the fewer and fainter the lines, until the three heads are almost nothing. On the mother's face the wash is a thin glaze laid OVER a normally painted face: warm rosy flesh showing through, never grey, never ashen.

PEOPLE. Image 3 is the costume sheet of the laughing adults, drawn from this same low angle: use it for their clothes, shoes, hands, the fan, the enamel mug and the way their heads are left as a few pale lines with nothing inside; use its older woman with the fan for the grandmother, its young woman in the dress for the aunt, its tall man in the vest with the mug for the uncle; leave out its old man with the cane. Mama, 1986, aged 33: a Chinese woman, young and attractive, smooth unlined warm skin; a soft oval face with a gently pointed chin, long almond dark eyes, clearly drawn dark straight-ish eyebrows that read strongly behind her glasses, a straight nose, a full mouth; glossy jet-black hair in a soft perm of loose springy curls, side-parted, ending at the jaw (never longer); thin round wire-rim glasses. The straight strong shoulders and upright carriage of a former competitive swimmer. Summer clothes, Shanghai 1986: a plain white short-sleeved cotton blouse with a small soft collar, loose dark trousers, black cloth shoes. No wrinkles, no sagging, no grey hair: 33. Image 4 is Mama's accepted face sheet: reproduce THAT woman, a few years younger. Use the images for likeness only; repaint in this painting.

SUBJECT. A kitchen in Decatur, Illinois, 1990, a bright morning. A Chinese woman of about 38, seated and leaning forward, seen very close and face-on from the eye level of the small daughter who stands between her knees: her head and shoulders fill the middle of the frame. Both her upper arms leave the picture at the two bottom corners, reaching toward us: her hands, out of frame below, are on the child's face. Behind her, the back wall of the kitchen: at the left a double-hung sash window over the sink, full of daylight; under it the window sill, the counter edge, a steel sink and one tall swan-neck tap; directly behind her head and to its right a white enamel stove with four ring burners and an upper cupboard above it; at the far right the side of a refrigerator with a long upright handle.

COMPOSITION. Follow image 1 exactly: the same camera, the same very large head in the middle of the frame with the eyes two fifths of the way down, the same shoulders across the bottom, the same window, counter, tap, stove and refrigerator in the same places. Image 1 is only a layout drawing from a 3D model: replace its mannequin with the real woman (the large dome round the mannequin's head is her hair: paint her own jaw-length permed curls, much smaller than that dome), replace its boxes with the real things named above, and do not keep its mechanical even line.

WHAT SHE IS DOING. She is getting her daughter's face right. With both hands (out of frame) she is setting the child's cheeks, and she is watching the result the way a swimmer on the blocks watches the water. Her head is perfectly still, tipped forward a very little. Her eyes look just below the lens, both irises lowered a fraction and converged on the child's mouth, steady and exact. Her lips are together and level, her jaw loose, her brows resting. She is not smiling and not frowning and not posing for anyone: all the life in the face is in the eyes. It is the same kind of face her daughter has, and she has no idea that her own is doing it.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. Image 2 shows it: the daylight is BEHIND her. The window panes at the left, the sill and the strip of counter and sink under the window are NOT PAINTED: bare cream paper left blank, with only thin ink outlines. No yellow, no white paint, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom: light is simply where the brush did not go. (the glazing bars and the tap are thin ink lines on the blank paper; nothing is seen outside the window). Where the sun passes over her from behind, it leaves only the top surface of her two shoulders as bare paper. Everything else, her face, her hair, the stove, the cupboard, the refrigerator and the wall, is in shade: one even transparent warm umber ink wash, the ink lines showing through it, nothing in it darker than a mid brown, no black. On her face the wash is a thin glaze laid OVER a normally painted face: her warm rosy flesh colour and a little warm blush on the cheeks still show clearly through it, never grey, never ashen. Image 4: his back-of-head sheet, THE hair anchor; his face is never shown. Image 5: his over-the-shoulder hair sheet; his face is never shown. Image 6: his hands and forearms sheet, no bracelet.

A painting on cream xuan paper, wide 16:9, in one hand: fine-line baimiao ink outlines and transparent ink wash, the paper grain and a few long paper fibres showing through everywhere.

SUBJECT. The living room of a 1950s split-level house in Morton Grove, Illinois, on a November afternoon about 2007, about half past three, low sun. A three-seat FLORAL couch (faded dusty-rose and cream flowers with green leaves) stands against the front wall, and right beside its end a big picture window with the low afternoon sun coming in. The ceiling above is vaulted. A young Chinese woman sits forward on the couch cushion next to the window, looking up. A young man stands in front of her, leaning in, his back to us, and hands her a folded WHITE cotton sweatshirt, lying folded flat as a neat square, and on its front a round seal printed in DARK BLUE: a simple roundel, a plain double ring with no letters, no words, no numbers in it (the ring is plain or carries only small dots), and inside it two tiny simple standing figures side by side. Both of them hold it: his hands on its near edges, hers closing on its far edges. Behind her: the couch back and arm, the window frame and its drape pulled back, a bit of the floor and a rug.

COMPOSITION. Follow image 1 exactly: we look over his RIGHT shoulder from behind and above it: the back of his head large and soft in the foreground at the upper left, his right shoulder and right arm reaching across the lower left to the sweatshirt; she sits beyond him, centre right, her face upper middle, looking up at him; the window at the upper right. The same camera, the same perspective, the same positions and sizes. Image 1 is only a layout drawing from a 3D model: replace its mannequins with the real people and its blocks with the real couch, window, sweatshirt and room, and do not keep its mechanical even line. Ignore the flat block on the woman mannequin's forehead: she has no fringe. The disc on the sweatshirt in image 1 is the seal. Her two hands close on the far corners of the folded sweatshirt, thumbs on top, five fingers each; his right hand holds its near left corner, his bare forearm with dark forearm hair reaching in.

WHAT SHE IS DOING. She is taking the gift and looking up at him, past it. Her head is still, tipped up toward him; both irises are raised to where his eyes would be, just above and left of us, bright and fixed, the way a child looks when she is counting. Her lips are together and level, her jaw loose, her brows resting, the faintest lift at their inner ends. She is not smiling and not frowning and not posing.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. Image 2 shows it: white and pale = light, grey = shade. The low sun through the picture window falls across her face, her hands and the sweatshirt: those sunlit parts are NOT PAINTED: bare cream paper left blank, with only thin ink outlines; her face in the sun keeps only the faintest warm flesh tint and blush and crisp line, never grey. No yellow, no white paint, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom: light is simply where the brush did not go. The window glass is bare paper. Everything out of the sun, his head, his back and shoulder, the couch's shaded side, the floor, lies under one even transparent warm grey ink wash, lines showing through; his back and head are the deepest, but never black. The sun/shade boundary is a clean, slightly soft wet edge. In each of her eyes one small crisp catch-light of bare paper, squarish like the window, on the same side in both eyes. Do not draw any dust in the air.

At the right of the bookshelves, a very wide doorway into the hall (its glazed doors folded back out of sight), dim; her mother stands in it, full figure, small in the frame, at its left side, having just come in. In the left foreground the arm and seat of a cushioned couch; in the right foreground an upholstered armchair standing in the sun, and beside it, end-on, a wicker lounger. Old wooden floorboards.

WHAT THEY ARE DOING. The child has not noticed anyone: her head is bowed, her eyes down on the pieces of paper in front of her, her hands on the table among them. The mother has stopped on the threshold in the first half-second of seeing this: her right hand has just caught the edge of the door frame at shoulder height, her left arm hangs, her weight is still on her front foot. Her head is tipped slightly forward and both her eyes are fixed on the child and the paper; her eyebrows are just beginning to rise and her lips have just parted to speak: "What on earth are you doing?" SUBJECT. The living room of a 1930s apartment flat in Shanghai, a clear winter morning, 21 December 1986, about half past nine. We look steeply down through the eyes of a three-year-old girl who sits cross-legged on the floor at the corner of a low wooden coffee table, her eyes only a hand's width above the table top. We do not see her head or face; only her small hands come in at the bottom edge. The table top is worn varnished wood. At the upper left of the table stands one plain undecorated white porcelain tea mug of green tea (no painted pattern) with a thin thread of steam rising from it, its round porcelain lid lying off beside it (a plain flat lid with a small knob, no feet). All over the far part of the table and on the floorboards beyond its right edge lies the drift of torn paper she has made over the morning: many, many torn pieces of every size, halves, quarters, strips, and fingertip confetti, overlapping, tipped up on their edges, curled, scattered thickly and messily, with small heaps where they gathered. They are torn paper, not leaves: blunt, irregular, roughly four-sided pieces with soft frayed edges, no pointed tips. Below the near edge of the table at the lower left and right, the floor is littered with more of it. In the middle of the frame she holds ONE WHOLE fresh sheet of the paper, a soft upright rectangle about the size of a postcard, nearly flat and low over the table, by its two near corners.

COMPOSITION. Follow image 1 exactly: the same camera, the same perspective, the same positions and sizes of the mug, the lid, the table edges, the floor, the whole sheet and her two hands. In image 1 the cylinder at the upper left is the tea mug (the thin line rising out of it is the steam), and the flat disc beside it is its lid lying on the table (ignore the three small marks under it: the lid has no feet); the large slanting plane is the table top, the plane at the right and the lower left is the floor below it; the many small irregular shapes are torn pieces of paper: paint each as real torn paper, irregular, soft, tipped and overlapping, none a neat rectangle, and paint MORE of them than image 1 shows, messier, thicker on the floor. The small rounded shapes at the bottom edge are her hands (and at the lower left her knee in padded trousers). The big upright rectangle in the middle is the one whole sheet she holds: keep its size and position exactly; its four edges are the straight mill edges of a fresh sheet, not torn.

WHAT SHE IS DOING. Her two small hands come in at the bottom edge, one at each near corner of the sheet: the thumb of each hand on top of the sheet, the forefinger under it, pinching the corner; the other fingers loosely curled. She is holding it still for a moment, about to make the first tear down the middle.

LIGHT, the most important thing in the picture. Low winter sun comes from tall windows out of frame. Image 2 shows where it falls (its pale shapes): across the far part of the table top and on the floorboards beyond the table's right edge, cut by the long dark bars of the window shadows. Those sunlit parts are NOT PAINTED: bare cream paper left blank, with only thin ink lines for the wood grain and board joints. The paper is caozhi, the rough hand-made toilet paper of 1980s Shanghai, in loose flat sheets about the size of a postcard (no roll, no print, no perforations): thin, soft, limp, a faint warm off-white with a few tiny darker straw flecks in it and a crêped, fibrous texture; every torn edge feathered and slightly wavy with hair-thin fibres standing out. This sheet is the richest and most carefully drawn thing in the picture, with the finest line; its crêped texture shown by faint short strokes and a few straw flecks; even though it is in shade, it keeps a thin margin of clean bare paper round its edges so it seems lit from within. The drift around carries the same paper, drawn more simply. The mug, the table and everything else carry no colour of their own.

THE CHILD (only her hands, and perhaps a knee and the cuffs of her sleeves, are seen). A three-year-old Chinese girl: small chubby dimpled toddler hands with five short fingers each; the slightly long cuffs of a padded cotton jacket in a faded pale red-and-white small gingham check over her wrists. The nearest woman (hair in a low bun, a white cotton kitchen jacket, a long apron) has her head bowed and her two palms pressed tightly together under her chin, fingers straight up, praying silently: her ten fingers drawn with care, the two thumbs side by side against her chest. Behind him a woman in a dark cardigan over an apron has her hands clasped hard together low in front of her, head bowed. REFERENCE IMAGES. Image 1: the layout drawing from the 3D set: camera, composition and the outline of every person and object (real body shapes, eyes aimed where each person looks; lines only, no shadows drawn). Image 2: the same view as evenly lit clay in the REAL colours: clothes in their real costume colours, skin and hair; wall art, book spines and clothing logos are the real fixed images; no cast shadows. Image 3: the light map: white = in the light, pale grey = weak light, mid grey = shade (where the light falls, not how dark the picture is). Image 4: the girl's face sheet at age 10 (her face; resting faces only). Image 5: the mother's face sheet (identity; here about forty, in a winter coat). Image 6: the old woman's costume sheet (her face is never drawn).

A painting on cream xuan paper, wide 16:9, in one hand: fine-line baimiao ink outlines and transparent ink wash, the paper grain and a few long paper fibres showing through everywhere.

SUBJECT. The produce aisle of a plain neighbourhood supermarket in Skokie, Illinois, in 1993, under rows of bare fluorescent tubes. A long grocery shelving unit (plain jars, tins, boxes; large plain cartons on top), a pallet of big plain cardboard melon cartons narrowing the aisle, a low produce island bin with mounded melons, cabbages, a heap of artichokes and pale spiky romanesco; a white drop ceiling with chain-hung tube strips; bare smooth concrete floor. No awnings, no banners, no signs, no price cards with writing. A moment of action. The ten-year-old girl had stopped dead in the middle of the aisle with an artichoke, blocking an old woman's cart. MID-SWING: Mama, close behind her, has hooked her right arm round the girl's back and under her left arm, her right hand spread flat on the front of the girl's ribs, clamping her against her own hip, and has lifted her off her feet: the girl's feet dangle a hand's breadth above the floor, knees soft, toes down, as Mama swings her aside toward the island. The girl still clutches the artichoke at her stomach in both hands, eyes on it. (The last two paintings missed this: her FEET MUST BE IN THE AIR, both soles clearly above the floor with a gap of bare floor under them, toes pointing down; she is carried on Mama's hip, not walking.) Mama looks back at the old woman and holds her LEFT hand out low toward her, palm up, open, fingers extended along the free lane: "go ahead". The old woman and her cart wait behind, now in clear view.

FRAMING. Follow image 1 exactly (a 32 mm lens, the camera 1.30 m above the floor, looking slightly down): Little Jade's head at the upper middle; the old woman's head (face unreached) at the upper middle; Mama's head at the upper middle; Little Jade's left hand at the centre; Little Jade's right hand at the centre; the old woman's right hand at the upper middle; Mama's left hand at the upper left; Mama's right hand at the centre; M1's camera line pulled back, wider: the girl lifted off her feet, her dangling feet a hand's breadth above the floor in frame; Mama close behind her; the old woman and her cart behind them in clear view.

Images 1-3 come from a 3D model of the real place. Image 1 (lines) fixes the camera, the composition and the outline and size of every person and object. Image 2 (clay) shows every surface in its REAL colour: the clothes are in their real costume colours, the people are real body shapes (not mannequins), the eyes are aimed exactly where each person looks, and any wall art, book spine or clothing logo is the real, fixed image that must reappear unchanged. Image 3 says only where the light falls, not how dark the painting is. Paint real people and real things over them; do not keep the model's even mechanical line or its flat clay shading. Motion is shown only by the poses: the lift, the dangling feet, the open hand. No motion lines, no blur.

THE HANDS (count every finger). Mama's right hand lies flat and spread on the girl's ribs, carrying her; her left hand is open palm up, offering the lane. The girl's two hands cradle the artichoke against her stomach, palms under and round it. The old woman's two hands are wrapped round the cart's red handle grip at navel height, elbows close to her sides. Her hands are a ten-year-old's: small, short fingers, short clean nails, bare forearms; five fingers on each hand, each with its knuckles.

WHERE EACH PERSON LOOKS. The girl's eyes stay down on the artichoke at her stomach, as if nothing were happening to her. Mama looks back over her shoulder at the old woman with the cart. The old woman's head is turned toward them (face unreached).

HELD THINGS. Little Jade's left hand and her right hand hold the artichoke (cradled: palms and fingers round its sides and under it, the thumbs on the near flank), supporting its weight; the old woman's left hand and her right hand hold the cart's red handle grip in a full, relaxed grip, supporting its weight.

LIGHT. Even light from rows of fluorescent tubes overhead: no direction, almost no shadow. The tubes themselves are NOT PAINTED, bare paper with thin outlines. Everything else, ceiling, shelves, cartons, floor, cart, the old woman, the produce, the coat and the clothes, is under one even transparent pale flat GREY ink wash: a cool neutral grey like diluted ink, never beige, never sepia, the same value everywhere, ink lines showing through, no local colour. On skin the wash is a thin glaze over normally painted warm rosy flesh, never grey. No black, no cast shadows.

THE ONE THING SHE IS ATTENDING TO. The artichoke at her stomach, small in this frame: A real globe artichoke about 11 cm across, the size of a large orange: round seen from above, squat, with about thirty broad, thick, fleshy BRACTS that wrap the head and overlap like roof tiles. Each bract is a wide cupped scale, its tip broad with a V-shaped NOTCH, a tiny sharp point in the notch and two or three small ragged teeth on each shoulder. The outer bracts are widest and stand a little open; the inner ones close over the top, which is CLOSED, with only a small pit in the middle. Colour: cool sage and grey-green faces, paler and yellower toward the base, violet-tinged tips and edges, fine parallel veins. NOT a cabbage, NOT a rose, lotus or succulent, NOT a pine cone. It is the only object painted in full local colour and full depth, with the finest, most loving line, bract by bract, like a botanical painter; modelling by transparent colour, not dark shadow. Round it a thin margin of clean bare cream paper, so that it seems lit from within. Everything else stays line under wash with no colour of its own except faces and hands.

CLOTHES (the colours are the real ones, as in image 2). Little Jade: a loose pale blue chambray button shirt worn open like a jacket over a plain white T-shirt, sleeves rolled to the elbows; straight khaki-tan cotton trousers; white canvas sneakers; no print, no lettering, no jewellery, no glasses (NOT the age-5 white jacket with the orange band: the guide's white top with an orange band and its blue trousers are placeholders, paint the chambray shirt and khaki trousers). Mama: a plain knee-length mid grey wool winter coat, unbuttoned, over a cream blouse (the guide's maroon is a placeholder: the coat is grey); dark charcoal trousers; thin round wire-rim glasses; no rings. The old woman: a knee-length nubbly boucle car coat in slate grey with large round buttons, a pale blue cardigan collar; a thin sage headscarf tied under the chin.

PEOPLE. Little Jade at about age 10, Skokie, 1993: a Chinese girl in fourth or fifth grade, 1.38 m tall. LARGE round dark eyes set wide apart with thick dark upper lashes; distinct, fairly strong, straight dark eyebrows; a tiny button nose; a small soft mouth; soft cheeks with a wide warm pink blush; a soft oval face. Glossy jet-black hair, long and straight to the middle of her back: a small half-ponytail high at the back of the crown, long side locks, the fringe grown out into a few thin strands parted to both sides. She is 10: a child, not a teenager. Image 4 is her face sheet. THE MOTHER: Mama in 1993, a Chinese woman of about forty, young-looking, smooth skin: a soft oval face, long almond eyes with near-black irises, a straight nose, a full mouth, clearly drawn dark straight-ish eyebrows; thin round wire-rim glasses; glossy jet-black hair in a soft perm of loose springy curls ending at the jaw. The straight strong shoulders of a former swimmer; strong capable hands with short plain nails. Her face is drawn in full; image 5 is her face sheet. THE OLD WOMAN: small, rounded, about seventy-five, a slight forward stoop, patient. She stands close behind her cart, both hands wrapped round the red handle grip at about navel height, a hand's width either side of the middle, palms down and slightly inward, elbows bent and close to her sides, forearms near level, wrists straight, relaxed shoulders. The cart is an American supermarket cart of the period: a chrome wire basket with red plastic trim and a red handle grip, a fold-down child seat at the handle end, a wire bottom rack, four casters; a carton and a honeydew melon in the basket. No store logo, no lettering on it. She is under the same pale grey wash as the shelves, no colour of her own. Her face is not drawn: the SAME grey wash as her coat, only the cheek and jaw in one thin broken line, no eyes, no nose, no mouth, like a figure the painter has not reached yet. Not a mask, not a pale oval, not a blur. Image 6 is the old woman's costume sheet. Use the images for likeness only; repaint in this painting.

Not anime, not cel shading, not a photograph, not a 3D or digital render, no dramatic chiaroscuro, no black shadows, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom. No text, no captions, no subtitles, no letters, no numbers, no signature, no seal, no border, no frame: captions and labels are added later in code and are never painted. Hands: count the fingers (five on every hand) and keep each hand exactly where image 1 puts it; a hand that holds something supports it (fingers round it or the palm under it), nothing floats.

SUBJECT. A back yard in Mountain View, California, on an October morning in 2010, about half past ten, BEFORE a housewarming party: no guests yet. Wide from the far corner of the wooden deck, looking down the empty yard: the deck railing and the stairs at the left (the half-barrel of mint tucked in the corner behind the deck railing at the lower left, mostly hidden), the corner of the raised strawberry bed at the bottom right of the picture, the lawn, the clothesline, the tall wooden fence, and in the far corner the GIANT lemon tree, its canopy filling the whole top of the picture, hung with enormous lemons, each the size and shape of a POMELO (paint them as big pale-yellow pomelos, heavy, on short stalks). Under the canopy in front of the huge trunk, small in the picture: the host, a 27-year-old Chinese woman, turned three-quarters toward us, reaching up with her right hand for one pomelo-sized lemon hanging just above her; to her right (picture right) the childhood friend, his back three-quarters to us, looking up into the tree, holding a FROSTED PLEXIGLASS punch bowl (pale, milky, softly see-through, the lemons showing through it as soft yellow shapes) in both hands from below, two pomelo-sized lemons in it STACKED one on top of the other (not side by side): EXACTLY TWO lemons in the bowl, no more. His head is tipped up toward the fruit, turned away from us: paint his face as a plain featureless shape under the wash (hairline, ear and jaw in thin line only; NO nose, NO lips, NO eye drawn); no watch on his wrists. Nobody else: no guests, no poi, no first love.

FRAMING. Follow image 1 exactly (a 24 mm lens, the camera looking down): Jade's head at the upper middle; the childhood friend's head (face unreached) at the upper middle; the childhood friend's left hand at the upper middle; the childhood friend's right hand at the upper middle; a wide shot from the deck's far corner down the yard, tilted a little down: the deck railing and stairs at the left with the mint barrel tucked behind them, the corner of the strawberry bed at the bottom right, the two small figures under the giant tree in the upper middle, the canopy across the top edge.

Images 1-3 come from a 3D model of the real place. Image 1 (lines) fixes the camera, the composition and the outline and size of every person and object. Image 2 (clay) shows every surface in its REAL colour: the clothes are in their real costume colours, the people are real body shapes (not mannequins), the eyes are aimed exactly where each person looks, and any wall art, book spine or clothing logo is the real, fixed image that must reappear unchanged. Image 3 says only where the light falls, not how dark the painting is. Paint real people and real things over them; do not keep the model's even mechanical line or its flat clay shading.

WHAT SHE IS DOING. Reaching up for the lemon, her face lifted to it, absorbed and pleased; she is turned toward us enough that the small round NASA meatball patch on her jacket's LEFT chest (her own left, picture right of her zip) is clearly visible: a blue disc, EXACTLY the emblem in the top-right inset of image 4, small but readable. The friend looks up into the tree. Small, but her black clothes read.

THE YARD IS FIXED (the same in every shot, exactly where images 1-2 put it; never move, add or drop any of it): ONE low raised timber bed of strawberry plants (green leaves, small red berries, a few white flowers) on the lawn just off the wooden deck's far edge; ONE half whisky barrel of mint tucked into the little inside corner where the deck meets the stair railing, against both; the clothesline on its T-post; the tall wooden fences; and in the far corner ONE GIANT old lemon tree: a massive trunk about 80 cm thick (far too thick to put your arms round), forking low into four heavy limbs, standing a little out from the corner, its broad dense canopy spreading over the whole far corner of the yard and over both fences. There is no other planter, bed, pot or barrel anywhere.

WHERE EACH PERSON LOOKS. Jade looks at the point where image 1 aims her eyes (at the upper middle): her eyes and head turned to it exactly as in image 1, irises aimed at it (not at the camera unless that is the target). The childhood friend's head is turned toward the point where image 1 aims his eyes (at the upper right) (face unreached).

HELD THINGS. The childhood friend's left hand and his right hand hold frosted plexiglass punch bowl of picked lemons, supporting its weight.

LIGHT. A clear, fresh October morning. Image 3 shows where the sun falls (white) and the shade of the fence, the house and the big canopy (grey). The sunlit parts are bare cream paper with thin outlines and only the lightest local colour (leaves, lawn, pale yellow fruit, red strawberries). The shade a light, cool transparent blue-grey wash, the dappled shade under the canopy. No haze, no glow.

CLOTHES (the colours are the real ones, as in image 2). Jade: a THIN near-black zip-front jacket, long sleeves, worn unzipped but hanging nearly closed, the small NASA meatball patch on its LEFT chest (her own left), over a fitted black T-shirt of which only a narrow sliver shows; boot-cut black yoga pants, snug to the knee and flaring to a hem that covers the heel; SNEAKERS outdoors: plain black canvas low-top sneakers with white rubber soles, laced (NOT socks, NOT flats, NOT boots); thin dark rectangular half-rim glasses; the jacket hangs open over the waistband: NO BELT, no dress, no pendant, no jewellery; the black is soft layered ink wash with folds and seams readable, never a flat black hole. The childhood friend: a plain tan cotton shirt with the sleeves pushed up; dark charcoal trousers.

PEOPLE. Her small NASA meatball patch (blue disc, white lettering, red chevron) sits on the jacket's left chest exactly as image 2 shows it. Jade, 2010, age 27: a Chinese woman; an oval face with a softly pointed chin, almond eyes with deep near-black irises (almost as dark as her hair), dark, fairly strong, slightly asymmetric eyebrows (the one on the LEFT of the picture straight; the one on the RIGHT runs straight and then lifts into a soft arch), a straight nose, full lips. Thin dark rectangular half-rim glasses. Long black hair with NO fringe: an open forehead, parted slightly off-centre, swept to both sides in long soft face-framing layers with a loose wave, past the shoulders. Image 5 is HER FACE: her accepted face sheet. Though she is small in this picture, her face, glasses and hair are exactly that woman's (ignore the navy dress and the pendant she wears on that sheet); keep her natural, real face, do not idealise it. Image 4 is her costume sheet for this party (the jacket, its patch, the trousers).

SHE IS DRAWN LOUDER THAN EVERYONE ELSE. She alone is drawn with a slightly heavier, darker ink outline (about fifteen per cent thicker than every other line in the picture) and with washes one step richer: inkier blacks in her clothes with the small blue patch the one bright note, blacker hair, warm rosy skin, a little more colour in cheeks and lips. Not a caricature, not a different style.

The childhood friend, a man of 27, Ukrainian (Russian-speaking), about 1.85 m, tall and slim, short hair in the colour image 2 gives it (light brown); fine DARK-BLOND hair on his bare forearms. His face is never drawn: we see him from behind or turned away; if any of his head turns toward us it is a simple shape under the same wash, hairline, ear and jaw in thin line, no features, like a figure the painter has not reached yet (not a mask, not a white oval).

Use the images for likeness and layout only; repaint everything in this painting.

Not anime, not cel shading, not a photograph, not a 3D or digital render, no dramatic chiaroscuro, no black shadows, no glow, no rays, no haze, no bloom. No text, no captions, no subtitles, no letters, no numbers, no signature, no seal, no border, no frame: captions and labels are added later in code and are never painted. Hands: count the fingers (five on every hand) and keep each hand exactly where image 1 puts it; a hand that holds something supports it (fingers round it or the palm under it), nothing floats.
